content:
This year’s BuiltWorlds Robotics Top 50 List offers a revealing look at where construction robotics is gaining real traction—and what the next phase of automation may look like.

Across the Automated Machinery & Related Solutions category, the biggest theme is clear: robotics is moving beyond isolated demonstrations and into the workflows where labor constraints, safety risks, and repetitive work create the greatest opportunities.

In 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐡𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 & 𝐄𝐱𝐜𝐚𝐯𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠, autonomy is increasingly being delivered through retrofits, remote operation, and machine-control systems rather than requiring contractors to replace their fleets. That points to a market focused not just on technical capability, but on making automation practical for the equipment already operating on jobsites. 

Congratulations to Caterpillar Inc. Command, Gravis Robotics, Built Robotics, Teleo, HIVE, Komatsu Intelligent Machine Control, Xpanner, Pronto, and Bedrock Robotics!

𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 shows another compelling path forward. Remote-controlled and robotic systems are taking on hazardous, physically demanding work while allowing operators to work from a safer distance. Meanwhile, specialized approaches such as hydrodemolition demonstrate that robotics can improve not only productivity, but also the quality and precision of the work itself. Congrats to the teams at Conjet Group and BROKK!

And in 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭, a new category of opportunity is emerging. Autonomous haulers, mobile robots, robotic hoists, and AI-enabled logistics platforms are targeting one of construction’s most persistent inefficiencies: moving people and materials around the jobsite.

A final congratulations to Daedong Robotics, FloMobility, KEWAZO, GoLe Robotics, and Cyphra!

Taken together, this year’s honorees suggest that construction robotics is becoming less about the robot itself and more about reimagining how work gets organized around increasingly autonomous equipment. The winners may ultimately be the technologies that fit seamlessly into existing workflows—not the ones that simply look the most futuristic.

As these technologies move from pilot projects into everyday construction workflows, where will contractors see the biggest opportunity to put robotics to work next? Let us know your thoughts in the comments 👇 

Read the full BuiltWorlds 2026 Robotics Top 50 list: https://lnkd.in/gVYgMpcK

Evan Mendez, Jay Grewal and I are pleased to announce the launch of Aldaron, defining a new category of investing and portfolio value creation we refer to as transformation equity. Our mission is simple: we want to be the partner of choice to exceptional businesses in the U.S. to help them grow by using frontier technology to unlock their human capital. All of us are grateful for the opportunity to build what we think is a highly differentiated firm, alongside world-class talent we get to work with every day. 

Our core organization is centered around our Deployment Team, which consists of a hybrid group of both investors and engineers who sit at the same table, make decisions together, and operate as one aligned group. True alignment – among our team and with our partner companies – is critical in enabling businesses to undergo AI transformation successfully.

What we believe:
1. We believe AI transformation is most successful when done from a position of strength. That means we look to partner with high-quality businesses in established markets with strong management teams. We believe that what leads to the best output is pairing management expertise and operational rigor with our technical knowhow and implementation experience.
2. We believe that every business will have to undergo some sort of AI transformation. We have opinions on the markets, competitive landscapes, business models, and companies that are most able to benefit from it.
3. We believe in the power of using AI to drive growth, and we DO NOT believe “cost out” strategies are sustainable over the long term.
4. We believe you have to be 100% dedicated, long-term oriented, and fully aligned with the companies going through transformation. Therefore, we do not believe in outsourcing AI, fractional solutions, or short-term thinking.
5. We believe that great technology is downstream from value creation, which is downstream from great culture. That hierarchy, in that order, is the only way to make it work.

content:
Just stepped off the stage for the Sunday morning panel here at PTC, and the coffee is finally starting to kick in.

We spent the last hour talking about "AI to Build AI"—which is really just a fancy way of saying we are looking for ways to make data center construction less of a guessing game. Everyone in this industry knows we need more capacity yesterday, but you can’t get there if you’re still building using old-school manual tracking.

Big thanks to Reid Senescu from Doxel and Jason Mehlhaff from Layton Construction for the conversation. We got into the weeds on "Physical Intelligence"—using computer vision and automation to actually see what’s happening on-site in real-time so we can stop rework before it starts. It’s about giving our GCs the tools to be predictable, not just fast.

If your schedule hasn't completely imploded yet, there is a lot more coming up:
·      Monday, Jan 19 @ 9:30 AM: Make sure you catch our Co-CEO, Tag Greason, on Center Stage (Tapa 2 & 3). He’ll be "Rewriting the Playbook" on the new realities of digital infrastructure. I’ll be there in the crowd—come sit by me.
·      Tuesday, Jan 20 @ 3:00 PM: I’m back on stage at the MPCC (South Pacific 3) for "Colocation at Speed: Building Data Centers for Today's AI Demands." We’ll be talking about what it actually takes to move at the pace the market is demanding right now without breaking things.

If you see me wandering the Tapa Tower looking like I’m "buffering," please say hello. And seriously, for the sake of my holiday-addled brain, give me some grace and remind me of your name—it's been a long few months! 

Off to stand in line for Ice Cream  (or at least a very long nap).

content:
11 years ago, I started my company on an unemployment check.

I'd applied late. I told the man at the government office I'd lost my job, that I was sleeping at the hacker dojo, and I needed the $1,900 to buy some cameras that I would start an AI company with. I pitched him the idea for what eventually became Doxel AI — told him this would create lots of jobs one day if he let me in. I must've looked desperate, because he helped me out. 

I remember he said "Make us proud."

I didn't know anyone in construction or any investors. I was 24 and hadn't even held a job for more than six months. But I had a laptop. So I cold-emailed builders and stopped by their offices unannounced until one took a bet on me and wrote me a $120K PO for a pilot. 

I was terrified of the pilot going well — I didn't have enough money to scale the product if it did.

I went to my college professor for advice. He laughed, wrote me a check, and introduced me to Andreessen Horowitz. They didn't care that I had almost no work experience. They liked the idea and led our seed so we could go build it out.

Strangers helped in ways I didn't expect. A man sold me his Camry for $2,200 — heavily discounted — when he heard I was starting a company. An Uber driver in Kansas City overheard me talking about a deal we needed to win, ran out of the car as I stepped out at the airport, and said he'd pray for my company's success. A flight attendant once got a message to our lawyers mid-flight — through the cockpit — when the wifi died during a negotiation for a critical deal. 

Insanely talented people decided I wasn't entirely crazy and took a bet on building this company with me.

We have a long way to go. But off that $1,900 unemployment check and the bets of so many people along the way, today Doxel tracks construction for 4 of the 5 largest hyperscalers, 14 of the top 20 data center developers, 18 of the top 30 general contractors, 3 of the world's largest EV and battery makers, 2 of the world's top 5 pharma companies and 5 of the country's leading health systems.

Only in America.

Happy Independence Day!
